groups.title: Authentication Patterns
groups.question: Explain how you would authenticate users in a Node.js API with tokens.

followUps.JWT Structure & Verification: What does verifying a JWT signature prove, and what does it not prove?
followUps.Refresh Token Rotation: How does refresh token rotation limit the damage of a stolen refresh token?

evidence.text: A valid signature proves the token was issued by someone with the secret and wasn't changed.
It doesn't prove the token wasn't stolen, or that the user still exists or still has those permissions.
Verification should also check the expiry and the expected algorithm.

notEnough: Only saying verify the JWT without saying what verification proves.

misconceptions.text: Says the JWT payload is encrypted and hidden from the client.

evidence.text: Each time a refresh token is used, it's replaced with a new one and the old one stops working.
If an old refresh token is used again, that signals theft, and the server can revoke the whole token family.
A stolen refresh token therefore works at most once, until the real user's next refresh exposes it.

notEnough: Only saying refresh tokens are rotated without explaining how that limits damage.

groups.title: Password Security
groups.question: Explain how you store and check secrets like passwords and tokens safely.

followUps.Password Hashing with bcrypt: Why is a slow hash like bcrypt better for passwords than SHA-256?
followUps.Timing Attacks & Constant-Time Compariso: How can comparing secret tokens with a normal equality check leak information to an attacker?

evidence.text: bcrypt is deliberately slow and its cost can be raised, so guessing passwords takes far longer than with a fast hash like SHA-256.
It adds a random salt per password, so identical passwords hash differently and precomputed tables don't work.

notEnough: Only saying hash passwords with bcrypt without explaining why slow is good.

misconceptions.text: Says passwords should be encrypted so they can be decrypted later.

evidence.text: A normal equality check stops at the first differing character, so it takes slightly longer the more characters match.
An attacker who measures response times can guess a secret character by character.
crypto.timingSafeEqual compares in a time that doesn't depend on where the values differ.

notEnough: Only saying use timingSafeEqual without explaining what a timing attack is.

groups.title: Authorization & RBAC
groups.question: Explain how you control what each user is allowed to do in your API.

followUps.Role-Based Access Control: What is the trade-off between putting roles in the JWT and checking them in the database on each request?
followUps.CORS & Security Headers: What is a dangerous CORS setup for an API that uses cookies, and what do security headers add?

evidence.text: Users get roles, and each role allows a set of actions, which the API checks before acting.
Roles in the JWT avoid a database lookup per request, but stay valid until the token expires even if the role is removed.
Checking the database each time reflects changes immediately but costs a query per request.

notEnough: Only saying use roles without explaining the trade-off.

evidence.text: Reflecting any origin, or allowing a wildcard, together with credentials lets any site make logged-in requests and read the answers.
The API should allow only its own known frontend origins.
Security headers, for example via helmet, tell browsers to block framing, content-type sniffing and untrusted scripts.

notEnough: Only saying configure CORS and add headers without saying what's dangerous.

misconceptions.text: Says CORS stops tools like curl or other servers from calling the API.

groups.title: OWASP Node.js Security
groups.question: Walk through the most common security threats to a Node.js API and how you defend against them.

followUps.Injection Attacks & Parameterized Querie: How can raw SQL in Prisma bring back SQL injection, and how do you stay safe?
followUps.Rate Limiting & DoS Prevention: Why does rate limiting need a shared store when you run several Node.js instances?

evidence.text: Building raw SQL by putting user input into the string lets crafted input change the query.
Prisma's tagged $queryRaw template sends values as parameters, but $queryRawUnsafe or building the string yourself brings the risk back.
Parameters keep values as data, never as SQL.

notEnough: Only saying Prisma prevents injection without explaining when it doesn't.

evidence.text: Rate limiting caps requests per client in a time window, slowing down brute force and abuse.
With several instances, each in-memory counter only sees part of the traffic, so the real limit multiplies by the number of instances.
A shared store like Redis keeps one counter per client across all instances.

notEnough: Only saying add rate limiting without explaining the multi-instance problem.
